c.tagline: Emilia-Romagna's capital of Parmesan, prosciutto, and Verdi opera.

taxi.fareNote: Metered white taxis wait at ranks (the station and Piazza Garibaldi) or are booked by phone/app rather than hailed on the street; Uber is effectively unavailable, so use a licensed taxi or the local ranks.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; 113 reaches state police and 118 reaches medical emergencies directly.

avoid.reason: The area around the train station can feel sketchy late at night; keep usual awareness there.

hood_desc: The compact medieval heart around Piazza Garibaldi, the Romanesque Cathedral and pink-marble Baptistery, Teatro Regio, and the vast Palazzo della Pilotta; best for first-timers who want the sights, food halls, and elegant streets all on foot.

The lively quarter 'across the stream' (the Parma torrent), traditionally the artisan and working-class side, now full of aperitivo bars, trattorias, and students, with the leafy Parco Ducale on its edge; suits travellers after local nightlife and character.

A practical, multicultural residential district just north of the historic core around the railway station; convenient for arrivals and budget stays, with everyday shops and eateries rather than monuments.

A green, calm area southeast of the centre named for the star-shaped Farnese fortress (the Cittadella), now a public park with jogging paths; good for families and travellers wanting quiet and open space.
A relaxed southern residential neighbourhood of parks, sports grounds, and local trattorias away from the tourist core; suits budget-minded and longer-stay visitors after an everyday Parma feel.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: Buy tickets from tabaccherie, machines, the Roger app, or on board (small surcharge); a single urban ticket is about €1.50, with day passes available. Validate/stamp your ticket on boarding.
transit.hours: TEP city buses run roughly 5:30am to 9pm, with a few limited evening lines; taxis, cycling, and walking fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Compact and famously bike-friendly, Parma has no metro or tram - TEP buses plus the flat, walkable historic centre and shared bikes cover almost everything.

bus: Piazzale Carlo Alberto dalla Chiesa (coach & Flixbus stops)

transit.m: TEP city bus to Parma centre (~15 min)
Taxi to the historic centre (10-15 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; a cover charge (coperto) is often already on the bill, so rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Prosciutto di Parma
food.desc: Sweet air-dried ham aged at least a year in the hills south of the city, sliced tissue-thin and eaten alone or draped over hot fried dough.

places.name: Salumeria Garibaldi
places.note: Classic city salumeria slicing DOP ham to order, with plates to eat at the counter.

places.name: Antica Osteria Fontana
places.note: Historic wine-and-panini bar, the local standby for a plate of ham and a glass.

places.name: Sorelle Picchi
places.note: Salumeria out front, tiny trattoria behind; a Parma institution for cured meats.

food.name: Parmigiano Reggiano
food.desc: The city other great export, tasted young at 12 months and crumbly and crystalline at 36 or more, often served with balsamic or mostarda.

places.name: Caseificio Bertinelli
places.note: Working dairy with early-morning production tours and tastings of different ages.

places.name: Mercato della Ghiaia
places.note: Central market stalls with wheels of Parmigiano and regional cheeses to sample.

places.name: Trattoria Ai Due Platani
places.note: Historic 1920s trattoria built on Parmigiano cooking; also famous for zabaione gelato.

food.name: Tortelli d erbetta
food.desc: Thin pasta squares filled with ricotta and chard, dressed only with butter and a snowdrift of Parmigiano. Eaten with your hands on Saint John night.

places.name: Trattoria Ai Due Platani
places.note: Repeatedly listed among the best tortelli d erbetta in the province.

places.name: Ristorante Cocchi
places.note: Open since 1925, cooking the Parma canon from family recipes.

places.name: Angiol d Or
places.note: Fresh pasta made daily by the Dall Argine family, in the shadow of the cathedral.

food.name: Torta fritta
food.desc: Puffed pillows of dough fried in lard, torn open hot and stuffed with prosciutto, culatello or salame so the fat melts into the bread.

places.name: Osteria dello Zingaro
places.note: Salumi boards with torta fritta made to order, exactly as locals expect it.

places.name: Trattoria Corrieri
places.note: Bustling central trattoria known for torta fritta and cured-meat platters.

places.name: Angiol d Or
places.note: Serves torta fritta with a well-chosen selection of Parma salumi.

food.name: Anolini in brodo
food.desc: Tiny stuffed pasta coins filled with slow-braised beef and Parmigiano, floated in capon and beef broth. The Parma Christmas dish, served year round.

places.name: Ristorante Cocchi
places.note: Century-old kitchen whose anolini in capon broth are a benchmark.

places.name: Angiol d Or
places.note: Beef and capon broth anolini among the daily fresh-pasta options.

places.name: Trattoria Corrieri
places.note: Reliable central address for the full traditional Parma first courses.

food.name: Culatello di Zibello
food.desc: The prince of salumi, cured in the damp river fog of the Bassa Parmense; darker, denser and far rarer than prosciutto.

places.name: Antica Corte Pallavicina
places.note: Riverside estate with historic culatello cellars and a famous restaurant; day trip.

places.name: Salumeria Garibaldi
places.note: Stocks culatello and other Bassa cured meats sliced to order in town.

places.name: Sorelle Picchi
places.note: Small trattoria serving culatello plates with torta fritta and local wine.

food.name: Malvasia e Lambrusco dei Colli di Parma
food.desc: The local wines are lightly fizzy: aromatic white Malvasia and dark Lambrusco or Fortana from the hills, poured cold to cut the fat of the salumi.

places.name: Tabarro
places.note: Standing-room wine bar famous for natural and local pours with salumi.

places.name: Antica Osteria Fontana
places.note: Old-school osteria where the city drinks its frizzante wine by the glass.

places.name: Trattoria Ai Due Platani
places.note: Strong list of Colli di Parma bottles to go with the traditional menu.

food.name: Bargnolino
food.desc: Home-style Emilian digestivo made by steeping wild sloe berries in alcohol, sugar and spices; dark, bittersweet and poured after dinner.

places.name: Trattoria Corrieri
places.note: Traditional trattoria that finishes meals with house liqueurs.

places.name: Tabarro
places.note: Late-night wine bar with regional amari and digestivi.

places.name: Mercato della Ghiaia
places.note: Market stalls and nearby shops sell bottled bargnolino to take home.

landmarks: Cattedrale di Parma (Parma Cathedral)
A supreme Romanesque cathedral whose dome erupts with Correggio's vertiginous Assumption of the Virgin, a Renaissance illusion of saints spiraling into heaven.
Battistero di Parma (Baptistery)
An octagonal marvel in rose Verona marble by Benedetto Antelami, its tiers of loggias and medieval frescoes marking the passage from Romanesque to Gothic.
Palazzo della Pilotta
A monumental Farnese complex housing the National Gallery, archaeological museum and the astonishing all-wood Teatro Farnese of 1618.
Teatro Regio
Parma's hallowed 1829 opera house, home of the Verdi Festival, where the world's most demanding loggione judges tenors without mercy.
Basilica di Santa Maria della Steccata
A Greek-cross Renaissance sanctuary adorned with Parmigianino's celebrated frescoes of the wise and foolish virgins arching over the presbytery.
San Giovanni Evangelista
A church-and-monastery complex behind the cathedral, crowned by another visionary Correggio dome and flanked by a historic monastic pharmacy.
Camera di San Paolo
The private dining room of a Renaissance abbess, transformed by young Correggio into a playful pergola of putti and mythological lunettes.
Parco Ducale
The Farnese dukes' elegant French-styled gardens across the torrent Parma, a shaded expanse of fountains, plane trees and the pastel Palazzo Ducale.
Piazza Garibaldi
Parma's convivial main square on the old Roman forum, framed by the Governor's Palace, sundials, and cafés perfect for an aperitivo with culatello.
Castello di Torrechiara
A fairy-tale 15th-century castle above vineyards south of Parma, hiding the frescoed Golden Chamber celebrating a famous knightly love affair.

train.note: No international trains. Parma sits on the Milan-Bologna line with Frecciarossa and Italo high-speed services reaching Milan in about an hour and Bologna in 30 minutes, plus regional trains to Modena, Reggio Emilia and up into the Apennines toward La Spezia. The station is a 10-minute walk north of the centre. Booking opens around 120 days ahead.

bus.note: Coaches use the stop beside the railway station. TEP runs the provincial buses out to the Parmigiano and prosciutto country around Langhirano and Busseto; FlixBus covers the long-distance routes. For most Italian destinations the train is quicker.

ferry.note: Parma is inland in the Po valley with no navigable passenger route, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Modena
half.blurb: The birthplace of balsamic vinegar and Ferrari has a Romanesque cathedral, about thirty minutes from Parma.

half.name: Reggio Emilia
half.blurb: A Renaissance city surrounded by Parmigiano-Reggiano dairies lies roughly thirty minutes from Parma.

half.name: Busseto
half.blurb: Composer Giuseppe Verdi's hometown, with his childhood home and a small opera house, is about forty minutes north.

half.name: Fontanellato
half.blurb: A moated Renaissance castle, Rocca Sanvitale, sits at the center of a small village about twenty-five minutes away.
